title: Gauss-Wantzel Theorem: n-gon Constructibility
description: The Gauss-Wantzel theorem: a regular n-gon is constructible by compass and straightedge if and only if φ(n) is a power of 2, equivalently n = 2^a · p₁ · … · pₘ where p₁, …, pₘ are distinct Fermat primes. Proved: Fermat prime recognition, φ(p) = 2^(2^k) for Fermat primes, and constructibility/non-constructibility for all regular polygons up to 17 sides. Axiomatized: the cyclotomic field degree connection.

overview.historicalContext: On 30 March 1796, the 19-year-old Carl Friedrich Gauss woke up and, before getting out of bed, discovered that the regular 17-gon is constructible by compass and straightedge — a result that had eluded geometers for two millennia. This was his first major mathematical discovery, and he was so delighted that he decided to become a mathematician rather than a philologist. Gauss proved the sufficiency direction: if φ(n) is a power of 2, then the n-gon is constructible. The necessity (if constructible then φ(n) = 2^k) was proved by Pierre Wantzel in 1837 using his algebraic characterization of constructibility. Fermat had conjectured in 1640 that all numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1 are prime, but Euler disproved this in 1732 by factoring F₅ = 4294967297 = 641 × 6700417. No Fermat primes beyond F₄ = 65537 have been found in nearly 300 years, though it remains unknown whether there are finitely or infinitely many. The complete list of known constructible prime-sided polygons is {3, 5, 17, 257, 65537}.
overview.problemStatement: Characterize all n ≥ 3 for which the regular n-gon is constructible by compass and straightedge in terms of the arithmetic of n.
overview.text: The Gauss-Wantzel theorem gives a complete answer: a regular n-gon is constructible iff φ(n) is a power of 2, iff n = 2^a · p₁ · … · pₘ where p₁, …, pₘ are distinct Fermat primes (primes of the form 2^(2^k) + 1). The known Fermat primes are F₀=3, F₁=5, F₂=17, F₃=257, F₄=65537; it is unknown whether more exist.
overview.proofStrategy: The key chain: n-gon constructible ↔ cos(2π/n) constructible over ℚ ↔ [ℚ(cos(2π/n)):ℚ] is a power of 2 ↔ φ(n)/2 is a power of 2 ↔ φ(n) is a power of 2. The last equivalence uses the multiplicativity of φ and the formula φ(p^k) = p^(k-1)(p-1).
keyInsights: Fermat primes p = 2^(2^k) + 1 satisfy φ(p) = p - 1 = 2^(2^k), a power of 2 — this is precisely why they yield constructible polygons
If an odd prime q appears squared in n (q² | n), then φ(q²) = q(q-1) contains the odd factor q, making φ(n) not a power of 2 and the n-gon non-constructible
Products of distinct Fermat primes have totient equal to a product of powers of 2 (hence a power of 2), so products like 15=3·5, 51=3·17, 85=5·17 yield constructible polygons
The non-constructibility proofs use bounded exhaustion: compute φ(n) = m by native_decide, bound k ≤ e via pow_two_bound, then use interval_cases to check all candidates
The gauss_wantzel_theorem is the single axiom: it captures the cyclotomic field degree formula [ℚ(cos(2π/n)):ℚ] = φ(n)/2, which requires ~200 lines of Mathlib glue to prove from first principles

conclusion.summary: The Gauss-Wantzel theorem is formalized with 0 sorries and 1 axiom (the cyclotomic field connection). All five known Fermat primes are verified, constructibility is established for 10 specific polygon sizes, and non-constructibility is proved for 4 sizes.
conclusion.implications: The theorem shows that constructible polygons are completely determined by Fermat primes. Whether infinitely many constructible primes exist depends on whether there are infinitely many Fermat primes — a major open problem (no new Fermat primes have been found since F₄ = 65537 in 1732).
